title: Signs of the Hour and Resurrection
question: If no one knows when the world ends, why does the Quran describe it so often?
summary: Why the Quran hides the time of the Hour but never its certainty; the signs it names and those hadith add; the unmaking of the cosmos, the two blasts of the Horn, and its argument that the dead will rise.

cover.alt: A vast desert plain under a sky where the sun is half veiled and stars appear at the edges
cover.prompt: A vast empty desert plain at an uncanny hour, the sun low and half veiled in dark haze, early stars showing at the edges of the sky, distant mountains faint as wool, the sand perfectly still.

blocks.p: Few questions were put to the Prophet ﷺ more often than this one, and few got a shorter answer.

"Its knowledge is only with my Lord", said twice in a single verse. The same reply comes in Madinah, "Perhaps the Hour is near" (33:63), and in the early Makkan surah al-Nazi'at with a sharper edge: "In what [position] are you that you should mention it? ... You are only a warner" (79:43-45). The Prophet ﷺ is not given the date to keep secret. He is told he does not have it.

A sceptic will find this convenient. A prophecy without a date can never be falsified. And yet the Quran talks about the Hour constantly: *al-sā'ah* returns dozens of times, alongside other names that each catch one aspect of it: al-Qiyamah, the Standing; al-Qari'ah, the Striking; al-Haqqah, the Inevitable Reality; the Day of Judgment. Why so much description of something whose time is refused?

The Quran gives its reason in a startling verse: "Indeed, the Hour is coming - I almost conceal it - so that every soul may be recompensed according to that for which it strives" (20:15). The hiddenness is not a gap in the teaching. It is the teaching. A known date would divide life into a long holiday and a short panic. An unknown one asks every day to be lived as if it might be the last, which is also, for every individual, simply true. 31:34 puts the two unknowns side by side: Allah alone knows the Hour, and "no soul perceives in what land it will die".

So the Quran describes the end not to satisfy curiosity but to change the present. Its descriptions are almost always followed by the same turn: and then a soul will know what it has brought. Whether the Hour is near in years, no one can say. For each reader, it is never more than one lifetime away.

chapters.title: The Stranger Who Asked About the Hour

blocks.p: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab remembered the morning for the rest of his life. The companions were sitting with the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah when a man appeared whom none of them knew. His clothes were intensely white, his hair intensely black. There was no dust of travel on him, and yet no one in the city recognised him. He walked straight through the gathering, sat down knee to knee with the Prophet ﷺ, placed his hands on his own thighs, and began to ask questions.

blocks.alt: The simple mosque of Madinah in morning light, palm-trunk pillars and a roof of fronds
blocks.caption: The mosque of Madinah, where the stranger asked his questions.
blocks.prompt: The early mosque of Madinah in clear morning light, rows of palm-trunk pillars holding a roof of dried fronds, sunlight falling in bright strips across a sandy floor and woven mats, a mud-brick wall and palm trees beyond.

blocks.p: What is Islam? What is faith? What is *iḥsān*, excellence in worship? Each time the Prophet ﷺ answered, and each time the stranger said, "You have spoken truly", which puzzled them: he asked as if he did not know, and confirmed as if he did. Then: tell me about the Hour.

blocks.quote: The one being asked about it knows no more than the one asking.
blocks.by: The Prophet ﷺ, in Sahih Muslim

blocks.p: Then tell me of its signs. The Prophet ﷺ named two: that a slave woman would give birth to her mistress, and that barefoot, destitute shepherds would compete in raising tall buildings. The stranger left. After a while, the Prophet ﷺ asked 'Umar whether he knew who the questioner was. "That was Jibril. He came to teach you your religion."

This hadith, recorded by Muslim from 'Umar and by al-Bukhari in another version, is so central that scholars call it the "mother of the Sunnah". Notice where the Hour sits in it: at the end of a lesson on faith and worship, answered with an admission of not knowing, and followed by signs that are social, not cosmic. The world turned upside down, wealth without roots, people who reach for height before they have learned to stand.

word.nuance: In ordinary Arabic, *sā'ah* is an hour or a brief stretch of time. As a name for the end it carries suddenness: the Hour comes "as a glance of the eye or even nearer" (16:77). And it carries irony: when it arrives, people will swear they lived only *sā'ah*, an hour (30:55).

blocks.p: The Quran says plainly that some of the Hour's indications, *ashrāṭ*, have already come (47:18). The Prophet ﷺ himself, al-Bukhari and Muslim report, held up two fingers side by side and said that he and the Hour had been sent like these. Beyond that, it names only a handful of signs, and it names them briefly.

**The moon split.** Al-Bukhari and Muslim report from Ibn Mas'ud that the moon split in two in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime, at Mina, and that he said, "Bear witness." Almost all commentators read 54:1 as that past event; a few read it as still to come.

**The smoke.** "Watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke, covering the people" (44:10-11). Ibn Mas'ud, in al-Bukhari, explained it as the famine that struck Quraysh, when the starving saw something like smoke between sky and earth. Others, citing a hadith in Muslim that lists smoke among ten great signs, held it is yet to come.
**Gog and Magog.** The barrier built by Dhu al-Qarnayn holds them back "but when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level" (18:98), and then "they, from every elevation, descend" (21:96).
**The creature.** "We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth speaking to them" (27:82), when the word of judgment falls due.

**A sign after which faith is too late.** On the Day some signs come, "no soul will benefit from its faith as long as it had not believed before" (6:158). Al-Bukhari and Muslim report that the Prophet ﷺ linked this to the sun rising from the west.

**'Isa.** "Indeed, Jesus will be [a sign for] knowledge of the Hour" (43:61), a verse most commentators connect with his return, though some read it as his miraculous birth, proof that the dead can be raised.

chapters.title: What Hadith Add, and What Lore Invents

blocks.p: Most of the familiar picture of the end times comes from hadith. A report in Muslim from Hudhayfah ibn Asid says the Hour will not come until ten signs appear: the smoke, the Dajjal, the creature, the sun rising from the west, the descent of 'Isa son of Maryam, Gog and Magog, three great landslides, and a fire that drives people to their gathering place. Scholars later sorted the signs into "minor" ones, social and moral, many already seen, and "major" ones that will come close together at the very end. That classification is a scholarly tool, not a Quranic term.

blocks.p: **The Dajjal**, the great deceiver, is not named in the Quran. Al-Bukhari reports that the Prophet ﷺ said every prophet warned his people of him, that he is blind in one eye, "and your Lord is not one-eyed". In Muslim, memorising the first ten verses of Surah al-Kahf is given as protection from him. **'Isa's return** is reported in al-Bukhari and Muslim: he will descend as a just judge and break the cross. **The Mahdi**, a righteous leader of the last days, appears in reports in Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, but not in the Quran, nor in al-Bukhari or Muslim.

Then comes a third layer, which is neither Quran nor hadith: speculation. Every century has produced people sure that the Dajjal was a ruler of their day, that Gog and Magog were a particular nation, that the creature of 27:82 was a new machine, that the signs could be lined up to compute a year. None of this has any authority, and the hadith of Jibril stands against all of it. The Quran gives no complete sequence, the hadith lists vary, and scholars caution that the order between the major signs is only partly known.

blocks.note: On 43:61, many scholars, following reports from Ibn 'Abbas, read "knowledge of the Hour" as 'Isa's descent before the end. Others read it as his fatherless birth, a sign of Allah's power to raise the dead; a few, reading the pronoun differently, take it as the Quran itself.
blocks.title: Where scholars differ

chapters.title: When the Sun Is Wrapped Up

blocks.p: Surah al-Takwir is among the earliest revelations, and it was the Prophet's ﷺ own example of the Hour's terror: a report in al-Tirmidhi has him say that whoever wishes to see the Day of Resurrection as if with their own eyes should recite it, with al-Infitar and al-Inshiqaq. Twelve times a line opens with *idhā*, "when":

The order is deliberate. First the sky: the sun "wrapped up" like a turban rolled up and put away, the stars falling. Then the earth: mountains moved, seas "filled with flame". Then, between the cosmic lines, two small ones. "When full-term she-camels are neglected": the *'ishār*, camels ten months pregnant, the most precious property a desert Arab owned, left untended, because nothing anyone owns will matter. "When the wild beasts are gathered": even animals that flee one another huddle together.

Then the human scene. Souls "paired", each with its like. The buried girl, killed in infancy by a father ashamed of a daughter, is asked "for what sin she was killed": not her killer, but she, as if the question were for the whole world to hear. Records opened, the sky stripped, Hell kindled, Paradise brought near. And after twelve "whens", one answer: "A soul will [then] know what it has brought."

Other surahs add their own images. People will be "like moths, dispersed" and mountains "like wool, fluffed up" (101:4-5). The earth becomes "a level plain" with no hollow and no height (20:105-107), then "replaced by another earth" (14:48). The whole created order, which seemed permanent, turns out to have been a tent.

The *ṣūr*, the Horn, is mentioned ten times in the Quran. At the first blast, everything living in the heavens and the earth *ṣa'iqa*, falls dead or senseless, "except whom Allah wills". At the second, "at once they will be standing, looking on". Surah Ya-Sin adds the movement: "from the graves to their Lord they will hasten" (36:51), and the bewildered question, "Who has raised us up from our sleeping place?" (36:52).

blocks.note: Most scholars count two blasts, the one of death and the one of rising. Some, including Ibn Kathir, count three, reading the "terror" of 27:87 as a separate first blast. Who is excepted by "whom Allah wills" is debated: certain angels, the martyrs, or others. The angel who blows it is named Israfil in later reports, not in the Quran. Al-Bukhari and Muslim report that Abu Hurayrah said "forty" lay between the two blasts, and declined to say forty of what.
blocks.title: Two blasts or three?

blocks.p: How will bodies return? The Quran's recurring image is rain on dead land. "We have given life thereby to a dead land. Thus is the resurrection" (50:11); "thus is the resurrection" again in 35:9. A hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim draws the same picture: Allah will send down water from the sky and people will grow as plants grow; every part of a human being decays except one small bone at the base of the spine, *'ajb al-dhanab*, and from it the body will be reassembled.

Al-Bukhari and Muslim also report that people will be gathered barefoot, unclothed and uncircumcised, exactly as they were first made. The Quran says it in one line: "You have certainly come to Us just as We created you the first time" (18:48).

chapters.title: Who Will Give Life to Bones?

blocks.p: The objection is ancient, and the Quran quotes it in its strongest form. A man of Makkah, the commentators say, crumbled an old bone in his hand in front of the Prophet ﷺ and blew the dust into the air: who will bring this back?

The reply is an argument, not an assertion. "He forgets his [own] creation." Every person was once nothing: not dust, but not even that. If a human being can come from nothing to a body, a mind and a history, return from scattered dust is not the harder case. The same argument is made in 17:49-51: be stone or iron, or anything you think harder, "He who brought you forth the first time" will restore you.

Al-Hajj builds it out across a whole life: dust, a drop, a clinging clot, a lump of flesh, a child, maturity, old age, and then the earth, barren, quivering and swelling at the rain (22:5). The pattern of life from lifelessness is not hidden; it happens every spring. And al-Qiyamah takes the challenge to the smallest scale: "Does man think that We will not assemble his bones? Yes. [We are] Able [even] to proportion his fingertips" (75:3-4).

None of this proves the Resurrection. The Quran does not pretend it does; it is an event in the unseen, believed on the word of the One who promised it. What the argument does is remove the claim that it is impossible. If the first creation happened, the second is not absurd. What remains is the question of trust, and a question the Quran keeps asking: given what you have already seen, why is this the thing you find too hard to believe?

You might expect a religion that talks so much about the end of the world to breed people who stockpile and wait. The Prophet ﷺ pointed in the opposite direction. In a report in the Musnad of Ahmad and in al-Bukhari's *al-Adab al-Mufrad*, he said that if the Hour arrives while one of you holds a palm sapling in his hand, and he can plant it before it comes, let him plant it.

list: **In every prayer.** In the final sitting of the prayer, the Prophet ﷺ taught, in a report in Muslim, to seek refuge in Allah from the punishment of Hell and of the grave, from the trials of life and death, and from the evil of the Dajjal. Millions of Muslims say it daily.
**Surah al-Kahf.** Many Muslims recite al-Kahf on Fridays, and memorise its first ten verses, following the hadith in Muslim on protection from the Dajjal.
**Refuse the date-setters.** A Muslim who forwards a video calculating the year of the Hour is contradicting 7:187. The signs are reminders, not a calendar.

**Read the minor signs as mirrors.** Tall towers raised by people who have not learned humility, trust betrayed, knowledge lost: the question is not whether they are happening out there, but whether they are happening in me.

blocks.p: For a non-Muslim friend, this explains why end-times talk among Muslims can sound both vivid and oddly calm. The Hour is certain; its time is not anyone's business. The work in front of you is. The same Prophet ﷺ who described the Dajjal in vivid detail spent his years in Madinah building a community and settling disputes, and, the biographies report, planted with his own hands the palm saplings that bought Salman al-Farisi his freedom.
Al-Nazi'at ends its answer about the Hour with a single sentence about time:

All of history, every empire, every life, every long night of grief, will seem on that Day like an afternoon, or the morning of one. It is a hard verse and a merciful one. Hard, because the years we think we have are shorter than they feel. Merciful, because the suffering that seems endless is shorter too.

The signs, the Horn, the splitting sky: the Quran describes them so that a heart can do now what it will otherwise do too late, which is to see clearly. "A soul will [then] know what it has brought" (81:14). The invitation is to know it first, today, while what you bring can still be changed.

If you believe, the Resurrection is not a threat but a promise kept: the dead you love are not lost, and nothing done for Allah's sake has disappeared. If you are still looking, the Quran asks you only to weigh its argument fairly, and to notice that you are already living inside the question it raises: each of us will meet our own hour, whatever we believe about the last one. He who made you the first time has not forgotten how. Carry the verse with you:

quiz.q: When asked the date of the Hour, what was the Prophet ﷺ told to say (7:187)?
options: It will come in his lifetime
Its knowledge is only with my Lord
When every sign has been counted
quiz.why: 7:187: "Its knowledge is only with my Lord. None will reveal its time except Him." In the hadith of Jibril he said the one asked knows no more than the one asking.

quiz.q: What reason does 20:15 give for concealing the time of the Hour?
options: So that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for
So that only prophets know it
quiz.why: 20:15: "the Hour is coming - I almost conceal it - so that every soul may be recompensed according to that for which it strives." The hiddenness keeps every day morally serious.

quiz.q: Which of these end-time figures is described in hadith but not named in the Quran?
quiz.why: Gog and Magog (21:96), the creature (27:82) and 'Isa (43:61) appear in the Quran. The Dajjal is known from hadith, including al-Bukhari and Muslim.

quiz.q: How does the Quran answer the man who asks, "Who will give life to bones while they are disintegrated?" (36:78-79)?
options: It says the question is forbidden
He who produced them the first time will give them life
Only the soul returns, not the body
quiz.why: 36:79: "He will give them life who produced them the first time; and He is, of all creation, Knowing." The argument is from the first creation to the second.

reflect: The Quran hides the Hour's time but never its certainty. If your own hour came this year, what would you most want to have planted?
